scenes.text: You photograph your son on his first day of school. You cover his face with a sticker, and post it. Private, right?

Not quite. A stranger can give it to an AI that reads what's left: the name on his lunchbox. The street sign behind him. The face was never the leak. Strangers' Eyes shows you what that AI sees, before you post.

One: your device covers faces and private words with solid blocks, and strips hidden photo data. Two: Google's Gemini, in the cloud, plays the stranger, and sees only that cleaned copy. Three: your private list, home, work, child's name, never leaves your device. It checks how close the guess came, and never tells the cloud if it was right. Four: fix it, and attack again.
Now the real app, in Judge Mode, with Gemini Nano on, and a made-up family with a son called Lucas.
This castle photo has a lunchbox labelled Lucas. Your device finds the name and covers it, and Gemini Nano scans for clues, before anything is sent.
We took the cover off on purpose. A last checkpoint inspects every request to the AI. It found the name and stopped it. That copy never reached the attacker.

Cover back on, the copy goes out. These are real Gemini answers, recorded on November twenty-third and replayed. The AI recognised the castle. The app never shows where the AI thinks you are, only how close it came: within one kilometre of home, and of work. You can't cover a castle, so the app says: crop it, or don't post it.

Here a fix helps. The AI read a street sign and its house-number plate, and found the street, within five kilometres of home and work. The app covers both, then attacks again. Now it can only guess the city. But your work is in that city, so your device still flags it: still exposed, at city level.
Don't take our word for it. Prove it offline keeps the stranger's answer sealed. We cut the connection and open it: the guess is checked on this device. Zero cloud calls.
Last step: save a covered copy, rebuilt and checked again on your device. That's the copy you post.

We measured it. A made-up name on a card: the AI read it every time, even through a light blur. Under the solid box: never. On thirty-six new photos, it placed eight within five kilometres. And when a clue could be covered, the fix moved nine in ten out.

That's hybrid AI: the cloud brings world knowledge, your device keeps the secrets. Private steps run on Gemini Nano in Chrome, as you just saw, or on Apple's own model on iOS, shown here in the iOS Simulator. No on-device AI? Simple rules take over, never the cloud. Built on Firebase AI Logic.
A covered face isn't a hidden child. See what a stranger's AI sees, before you post. Strangers' Eyes.
